chunks.content: 1 Introduction Chemotherapy‐induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) is a common and distressing side effect for oncology patients [ , , ]. Nausea and vomiting in these patients can be acute (≤ 24 h after treatment) or delayed (> 24 h after treatment) [ ]. Unaddressed CINV affects patients' abilities to tolerate chemotherapy and can lead to worsening quality of life and performance status, anticipatory nausea, and result in dose reductions or early termination of chemotherapy [ ]. The management of CINV is complex, as it is impacted by both the emetogenicity of the chosen chemotherapeutic agent and the occurrence of two distinct pathophysiological phases (acute and delayed) which can result in different outcomes and require distinctive treatment approaches [ , ]. Therefore, organizations such as the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC) [ , ], the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) [ ], and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) [ ] have generated guidelines to aid clinicians in optimal prophylaxis of CINV. These guidelines recommend that when oncologic treatments are chosen, the emetogenic potential of chemotherapeutic agents should be assessed so that providers can prescribe appropriate prophylactic antiemetic agents [ , ]. Even with these guidelines, CINV remains an issue for many patients, prompting numerous investigations into potential risk factors for CINV, with the goal of determining a prophylactic strategy for medications. These factors include history of CINV with prior chemotherapy and/or perceived susceptibility to nausea, female sex, low chronic alcohol intake, and younger age [ , ] and have been used to assess patients' risk for the development of CINV [ ]. However, the patients' individual biology is not included in previous predictive algorithms. The pathophysiology of CINV, and nausea especially, is not well understood, though one proposed mechanism suggests that CINV is triggered by free radicals in the small intestine induced by chemotherapy. These free radicals, such as reactive oxygen species (ROS), cause release of serotonin and substance P from enterochromaffin cells [ , ], subsequently activating their respective receptors and inducing nausea and vomiting [ ]. Based on this mechanism, we have previously developed a hypothesis that a patient's risk of CINV is directly related to their efficiency in scavenging free radicals via glutathione (GSH), a major antioxidant, after exposure to chemotherapy. Specifically, we have focused on measuring recycling of GSH (GSHrc) as a mechanism by which cells detoxify the reactive oxygen species released after chemotherapy [ , ]. In brief, the method is based on enzymatic conversion of the bioactive probe hydroxyethyl‐disulfide (HEDS). Due to reported single‐nucleotide polymorphisms among the enzymes in the recycling process [ ], individual variation in the rate of GSHrc, and thereby detoxification, can affect ROS levels and in extension release of neurotransmitters which activate the emetic response [ , ]. We have previously described preliminary results for our development of the glutathione recycling (GSHrc) assay and outlined its relationship to CINV [ , ]. We developed a predictive model for chemotherapy‐induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) using data from 202 patients who received platinum‐based chemotherapy for colorectal, lung, esophageal, head and neck, and other non–hormone‐driven malignancies. These cancer types were selected to ensure balanced representation by sex and inclusion of all three commonly used platinum agents—carboplatin, cisplatin, and oxaliplatin. Our prospective analysis led to the creation of a risk score to estimate individual CINV risk. This model may support clinicians in making personalized decisions for the prevention and management of CINV. 1.1 Study Objectives The primary objective of this study was to develop a predictive model for chemotherapy‐induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) that integrates both clinical risk factors and a patient‐specific biological measure of glutathione recycling (GSHrc). We aimed to generate a practical risk score that can stratify patients by their likelihood of developing CINV after platinum‐based chemotherapy. With the larger cohort, we could utilize machine learning techniques, allowing for the inclusion of more variables to improve personalized prophylaxis and optimize supportive care for patients undergoing chemotherapy. 2 Methods 2.1 Patient Cohort Our prospective observational study was performed as a single‐center investigation conducted at Lankenau Medical Center through a collaboration between the Alliance Cancer Specialists oncology clinic and the Lankenau Institute for Medical Research (LIMR). Applying exclusion criteria (Figure ) and removing patients lost to follow‐up resulted in a cohort of 202 patients with analyzable data. Patients across all socioeconomic groups, races, and ethnicities were encouraged to participate. However, the population in our health system area is predominantly Black and White, with approximately 10% identifying as Hispanic, Asian, or other. Written and signed informed consent was obtained from all patients. Adults (> 18 years old) of both sexes were permitted following the protocol, and all patients had to be chemotherapy naive. Patients with a recurrence or a second primary were not enrolled in this study. All patients with a solid tumor and receiving a platinum‐based therapy were treated according to current medical standards; the medical staff had exclusive authority in recommending therapy based on stage of disease and/or co‐morbidities. Patients treated with a highly emetogenic chemotherapy (HEC) [ , ] including cisplatin, were given 0.25 mg palonosetron IV, aprepitant 150 mg IV, and 10 or 20 mg dexamethasone IV prior to chemotherapy (all antiemetic regimens given are described in Table ). Most patients treated with a carboplatin‐containing regimen (85%) received the agent at Area Under the Curve (AUC) 2, which is considered a moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (MEC) [ ] and given with a 2‐drug antiemetic preventive treatment (0.25 mg palonosetron IV and 10 or 20 mg dexamethasone IV) [ , ]. Oxaliplatin was given at either 85 mg/m 2 or 130 mg/m 2 depending on the regimen. This patient group received the same antiemetic regimen as patients treated with carboplatin AUC 2. All patients were given prescriptions to fill for ondansetron and prochlorperazine if treated with oxaliplatin or carboplatin (AUC < 4). Patients treated with cisplatin or carboplatin (AUC ≥ 4) were prescribed the same agents with the possible addition of olanzapine. All prescriptions were for pro re nata (PRN) use during the 24–96 h post‐treatment, and instructions were given by the medical oncology staff for dosing frequency. 2.2 Blood Samples and Patient‐Reported Outcomes Each patient donated a tube of blood (12 mg K 2 EDTA) the day of their first treatment. Blood samples were collected prior to antiemetics and chemotherapy, at the time medically necessary samples were obtained to determine eligibility for chemotherapy and were subsequently transferred for research analysis. Blood samples were analyzed within 1–2 h of collection using the glutathione recycling kit (Mynari Biomedical LLC) and mixed with the bioactive probe HEDS which is converted into mercaptoethanol (ME) through the enzymatic activities of the glutathione recycling pathway [ , , ]. The amount of ME produced was determined by adding Ellman's reagent to clarified reaction mixtures and measured at 412 nm in a spectrophotometer. Glutathione recycling (GSHrc) capacity was calculated by converting read‐outs to ME per millions of red cells [ , ]. GSHrc results obtained from chemotherapy‐naïve patients were used to predict the occurrence of delayed nausea during any of the subsequent planned treatment cycles. Patients self‐reported nausea symptom and severity using the Rotterdam Symptom Checklist (RSCL) [ ] directly prior to each cycle. Questionnaires were distributed and collected by a study coordinator, who was available to address study‐related questions. Delayed nausea was defined as symptoms occurring 24–120 h following chemotherapy. All patients included in the analysis were prospectively followed for the full duration of their planned treatment course. No changes to antiemetic regimens were made prior to the first report of delayed nausea. Nausea severity was dichotomized into two groups, none or mild and moderate or severe. Mild nausea corresponds to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grade 1, for which no intervention was required. Moderate and severe nausea corresponded to CTCAE grades 2 and 3, respectively, which necessitate changes in management or hospitalization. Reports of nausea were compared to those documented in the electronic medical records. 2.3 Statistical Methods Baseline characteristics were compared between groups using two‐sample t ‐tests, chi‐square tests of independence, and univariable logistic regression to display the effect size of each variable. To incorporate more predictors than the original binary cut‐point identified using CART, elastic net regression was used to build predictive models and a risk score. Elastic net regression with a logit link function was applied to estimate optimal coefficients while minimizing the risk of overfitting. The model incorporating the GSHrc score, age, sex, ethnicity, and treatment type was developed using Elastic Net regression. To assess calibration, the dataset was divided into ten groups based on predicted probabilities. The observed outcome incidence was then plotted against the mean predicted probability for each group. Calibration was further quantified using the expected‐to‐observed ratio (E:O) to detect under‐ or over‐estimation of risk, the calibration slope to assess overfitting or underfitting, and the calibration‐in‐the‐large (CITL) to evaluate systematic over‐ or under‐prediction. Model discrimination was measured using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). In addition, 95% confidence intervals for slope and CITL were calculated using logistic regression with predicted probabilities as the only predictor, and for AUC using Stata's roctab command. For internal validation, both 10‐fold cross‐validation and bootstrap cross‐validation were employed. The 10‐fold cross‐validation assessed out‐of‐sample performance by partitioning the data into ten subsets, iteratively training the model on nine parts and validating on the remaining part, and bootstrap cross‐validation was used to estimate model optimism without partitioning the dataset, improving the robustness of internal validation. Validation metrics included the root mean square error (RMSE) and the AUC to reflect both prediction error and discriminative ability. Once the model was validated, a risk score was constructed using the penalized coefficients from the Elastic Net regression. All continuous variables were standardized by Stata before fitting the Elastic Net model. Penalized coefficients were then transformed back to the original scale for the predictors for model presentation and risk‐score calculation. Each score was converted to a predicted probability using the formula: Predicted Probabilities = 1 (1 + exp. (−Risk Score)). The predicted probabilities from the risk score were then validated to ensure they matched the predictive model using a univariable logistic regression model, with nausea severity as the outcome. The risk score probabilities' discrimination and calibration were assessed by calculating the area under the AUC, slope, CITL, and O:E. These metrics matched the original elastic net model metrics. These probabilities were used to estimate the risk of moderate to severe nausea and to identify the corresponding predicted probability risk thresholds. Based on these thresholds, patients were categorized into low, medium, or high‐risk groups. All analyses were conducted using Stata 17.0 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX) and R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). 3 Results After applying exclusion criteria (see Figure ), the analyzed cohort consisted of 202 patients who had a median age of 66 years (range 25–91 years) and follow‐up information for the planned regimen. Younger patients were significantly more likely to report moderate/severe delayed nausea ( p < 0.0001, Table ) than older patients. Enrolled patients predominantly identified as White (81.7%) with Black patients constituting 16.8% of the cohort and the remaining 1.5% representing all other races. Race did not significantly contribute to delayed nausea ( p = 0.745, Table ). Forty‐six percent of participants were female and no significant difference in delayed nausea severity was observed between the sexes ( p = 0.485, Table ). Approximately half of all patients were treated with an oxaliplatin‐containing regimen and 32% of patients in this treatment group reported moderate/severe nausea. Moderate‐to‐severe nausea was reported by 29.6% and 6.7% of patients receiving cisplatin or carboplatin, respectively. Patients reporting moderate/severe nausea were more likely to have been treated with oxaliplatin than the other two agents (Table ). To determine the performance of the calculated risk score, predicted nausea was compared to experienced nausea within each risk score group. Overall, we found a good correlation between predicted and observed nausea in all risk score groups. Model calibration for delayed chemotherapy‐induced nausea showed good overall agreement between predicted and observed risks (Figure ). In the low‐risk group, the observed incidence was 11.3% compared to the predicted 8.8%. In the medium‐risk group, the model slightly overpredicted nausea (31.4% predicted vs. 25.8%) observed. Calibration was strongest in the high‐risk group where predicted (61.9%) and observed (64.0%) risk were closely aligned. 4 Discussion In this study, we present an improvement of our previously published findings on a blood‐based test designed to predict individual risk of delayed chemotherapy‐induced nausea. Elastic net modeling allowed for the inclusion of more variables and use of predicted probabilities on a continuous scale, resulting in higher accuracy in prediction of delayed chemotherapy‐induced nausea. The performance of the prediction algorithm increased the AUC to 0.809 compared to the AUC of 0.716 for the binary cut‐off analysis. Despite advances in the prevention of chemotherapy‐related side effects, CINV—particularly delayed nausea—remains a distressing and costly complication of cancer therapy [ , , , ]. Accurately predicting which patients will develop delayed CINV remains a major clinical challenge [ , ]. Identifying those at highest risk enables clinicians to apply aggressive prophylactic measures selectively, avoiding overtreatment of low‐risk patients. In addition to the considerable reduction in patients' quality of life [ ], the average national cost for an emergency department visit due to severe delayed nausea has been estimated at up to $15,120 [ , , ]. Consequently, multiple intrinsic (e.g., sex, age, race) and extrinsic (e.g., alcohol use, diet, smoking) risk factors have been investigated for their predictive value in CINV [ , , , ]. In our work, we excluded variables were the patients might be reluctant to provide accurate habits, such as alcohol consumption and dietary preferences. A strong prediction factor for CINV is previous CINV symptoms during previous cycles. Therefore, all patients were chemotherapy naïve at the time enrollment. Oxidative stress generated by chemotherapeutic agents in the upper small intestine has been proposed as a key mechanism underlying nausea and vomiting [ , ]. Based on this rationale, we developed the GSHrc assay, which previously demonstrated promising sensitivity and specificity in identifying at‐risk patients using a CART algorithm [ , ]. In the present study, we enrolled patients with solid tumors expected to benefit clinically from platinum‐based therapy. To minimize sex‐related bias—since sex is a known determinant of nausea risk [ , ]—we focused on non–sex‐specific cancers, yielding a balanced cohort of 202 patients (46% female; mean age, 66 years). Cut‐point analysis performed in Stata 17.0 using the Lui option [ ] replicated our earlier observation: patients who developed moderate or severe delayed nausea had lower pre‐treatment GSHrc scores compared to those with no or mild symptoms (1.58 vs. 1.76, p = 0.06). Although not statistically significant, this trend supports the GSHrc score as a potential predictor of delayed CINV. Next, we evaluated established risk factors to determine whether combining intrinsic factors could enhance predictive accuracy. Consistent with prior reports identifying younger age as a risk factor [ , , , ], patients who experienced moderate/severe nausea were significantly younger than those with milder symptoms (54.2 vs. 67.3 years, p < 0.0001). Chemotherapy type was also associated with nausea severity: patients treated with the moderately emetogenic compound oxaliplatin [ , ] accounted for 71.1% of moderate/severe cases ( p < 0.0001). Among cisplatin‐treated patients ( N = 27), 29.6% reported grade 2/3 nausea, representing 17.8% of all moderate/severe cases. As expected for a highly emetogenic chemotherapy (HEC) [ , ], all cisplatin‐treated patients received standard triple antiemetic prophylaxis with a 5‐HT 3 antagonist (palonosetron), an NK 1 antagonist (aprepitant), and dexamethasone. In contrast, carboplatin ( N = 75)—administered at AUC 2 (MEC) in 80% and AUC 5–6 (HEC) in 20% of patients [ , ]—was associated with significantly lower rates of delayed nausea (6.7% overall, constituting 11.1% of grade 2/3 cases). Notably, oxaliplatin‐treated patients ( N = 100) exhibited the highest incidence of delayed nausea (32%), accounting for the majority (71%) of grade 2/3 events ( p < 0.0001). This finding aligns with observations by Hesketh et al. [ ], who reported delayed nausea in 42.9% of oxaliplatin‐treated patients despite excellent acute‐phase CINV control using a two‐drug prophylaxis (5‐HT 3 antagonist plus dexamethasone). Predicted probabilities derived from our model were categorized into low‐, medium‐, and high‐risk groups (Table ) and compared with observed outcomes (Figure ). Patients with risk scores ≥ 60 were correctly classified as low risk, indicating adequate protection from current standard antiemetic regimens. Scores of 45–59 corresponded to a 25%–50% risk, consistent with previously reported rates of nausea among patients receiving MEC or HEC therapy despite guideline‐concordant prophylaxis [ , , , ]. Clinical trials suggest that these patients benefit from adding an additional antiemetic agent during subsequent treatment cycles [ , ]. In contrast, patients with risk scores ≤ 40 exhibited a predicted 70% and observed > 80% risk of developing delayed nausea, indicating the need for more intensive antiemetic prophylaxis. Our findings, consistent with prior reports [ ], underscore that oxaliplatin‐treated patients contribute disproportionately to delayed nausea incidence when treated with the currently recommended two‐agent regimen. Current prophylaxis guidelines for CINV are largely determined by the emetogenicity of the chemotherapy regimen [ ]. Although major oncology organizations [ , , , ] agree on best practices for both acute and delayed CINV prevention, nausea—more frequent and impactful than vomiting—remains insufficiently controlled. This challenge is compounded by the subjective nature of nausea assessment, in contrast to the objective measurement of vomiting frequency and duration. Incorporating objective biomarkers such as GSHrc, alongside intrinsic factors, may enable a more personalized and precise risk prediction for delayed nausea, reducing bias from patient‐reported measures. Given the differing biological half‐lives of platinum agents, glutathione recycling may play a significant role in patient susceptibility. Carboplatin and cisplatin exhibit half‐lives of 1–2 days, whereas oxaliplatin persists for approximately 5 days. Thus, patients with slower GSHrc rates receiving oxaliplatin may experience prolonged oxidative stress, leading to sustained enterochromaffin cell injury and neurotransmitter release. Such patients may benefit from extended or intensified antiemetic coverage after infusion. Our future goal for the project is to determine the effect of additional antiemetics and the effects on severity and duration of symptoms. Furthermore, the GSHrc test could promote adherence to prescribed oral antiemetics by providing an objective rationale for their continued use. 4.1 Limitations This study has several limitations. First, it was conducted at a single tertiary teaching hospital located in a suburb of Philadelphia, PA, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to broader populations. Second, the outcome measures were based on patient self‐reports. Although we compared patient‐reported outcomes with documentation of nausea symptoms in medical records and adjustments to antiemetic regimens, recall and reporting bias may still have influenced the results due to memory limitations and the time constraints of clinical documentation. Additionally, while all patients received antiemetic therapy consistent with the standard of care—based on the agent with the highest emetogenic potential—and no modifications were made to regimens prior to reported nausea symptoms (as described in the Methods section), we cannot be certain about the extent to which patients used their prescribed PRN antiemetics. Patients who were predicted as medium/high risk of developing delayed CINV but never reported symptoms could have been compliant with their antiemetics and therefore able to prevent any experience of CINV. Third, no external validation was performed to assess the generalizability of the findings to other populations or clinical settings. Although statistical evaluation of the risk score suggests that the findings may be reproducible in similar patient cohorts, a dedicated validation study is needed to confirm these results and reduce potential sources of bias. Future prospective studies are recommended to include a more diverse racial distribution and collect more detailed treatment data, particularly regarding the use of rescue medications. 4.2 Implications of Findings Delayed chemotherapy‐induced nausea remains a major unmet need in supportive oncology care, frequently persisting despite guideline‐recommended antiemetic prophylaxis. Existing risk models, based primarily on demographic and treatment‐related factors, offer limited predictive accuracy. This study introduces a blood‐based glutathione redox cycling assay as an objective biomarker to identify patients at high risk for delayed nausea following platinum‐based chemotherapy. When integrated with clinical variables, GSHrc produced a validated risk score that stratified patients into low‐, intermediate‐, and high‐risk groups, with clear implications for individualized prophylaxis. High‐risk patients—regardless of the emetogenicity of the chemotherapeutic regimen—showed poor symptom control under standard antiemetic protocols and may benefit from intensified preventive therapy. The addition of an NK1 antagonist as a third agent in the antiemetic mixture prior to chemotherapy infusion or a transdermal patch for long‐term delivery of a 5‐HT3 antagonist could be effective approaches to eliminate delayed nausea among the high‐risk patients. Future prospective studies using these agents among high‐risk patients will be needed to ensure efficacy. Incorporating redox‐based biomarkers into CINV risk assessment may enable precision‐guided prevention, enhance patient quality of life, and reduce healthcare utilization associated with uncontrolled nausea. 5 Conclusions Integrating individual patient biology into a multifactorial predictive algorithm enhances the accuracy of identifying those at risk for delayed chemotherapy‐induced nausea. This personalized approach enables clinicians to proactively deliver intensified antiemetic therapy to high‐risk patients, thereby reducing delayed nausea, improving quality of life, and supporting adherence to potentially life‐saving chemotherapy regimens. Introduction Oral mucositis (OM) is among the most debilitating complications of cytotoxic chemotherapy in the majority of patients receiving cancer treatment [ , ], it impairs essential functions such as mastication, and phonation, leading to malnutrition and systemic deterioration [ , ]. The prevalence of OM ranges from 40% to 100% in those receiving various chemotherapy regimens [ , ]. Several commonly used chemotherapeutic agents, such as platinum, 5-fluorouracil, and methotrexate, induce mucosal damage through direct cytotoxicity and disruption of the microbiome [ ]. The oral cavity hosts a complex homeostatic microbial ecosystem whose members maintain symbiotic relationships with the host by supporting immune regulation and epithelial barrier integrity [ ]. However, disruptions in the equilibrium of the oral microbiota drive pathogenic shifts, to favour opportunistic pathogens such as Enterobacteriaceae that exacerbate mucosal damage, while depleting commensal Streptococci [ – ]. The extensive proliferation of opportunistic pathogens can lead to the formation of biofilms, which inhibit the colonization of normal flora and further disrupt the microecological balance, thereby increasing the duration of OM [ ]. In addition, the exudates of localized ulcers that occur in OM provide nutrients for opportunistic pathogenic bacteria. Moreover, the alteration in the pH level in the ulcerated area may further destabilize the microbial equilibrium [ ]. This ecological shift synergizes with chemotherapy-induced impairment of epithelial repair mechanisms manifested by abnormalities such as mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance, thus creating a vicious cycle of mucosal breakdown [ ]. In addition, metabolic reprogramming of epithelial cells under inflammatory stress can concurrently impair their repair capacity, amplify oxidative damage, and perpetuate the cycle of tissue degradation, which is closely related to the development of oral microbiota dysbiosis [ , ]. However, the role of oral microbiota dysbiosis in the induction or progressing of metabolic reprogramming in oral epithelial cells has not been thoroughly characterized [ ]. The metabolic products of certain bacteria, including proteases and endotoxins, can harm mucosal epithelial cells and exacerbate OM [ ]. Existing research has demonstrated that in the context of intestinal disease, the metabolic products of pathogenic bacteria can directly interfere with the metabolic processes in host cells [ ]. Given the close association and functional similarities between the oral and intestinal epithelia, analogous mechanisms may exist in the oral epithelium [ , ]. When the microbiota becomes dysregulated, the abundance of pathogenic bacteria such as Fusobacterium nucleatum increases, leading to an increase in the production of their metabolites, such as propionate [ ]. This process results in inhibition of the activity of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes in epithelial cells, thereby forcing these cells to switch to glycolysis for their energy supply [ ].On the basis of our previous experiments, we confirmed the existence of significant disruption of the oral microbiota (dysbiosis), accompanied by increased glycolysis in epithelial cells. In addition, oral microbiota dysbiosis is a critical influencing factor for metabolic abnormalities in epithelial cells. These findings underscore the need for interventions that simultaneously restore the oral microbial ecology to improve the metabolic function of epithelial cells to achieve sustained tissue repair [ , , , ], which constitutes an effective strategy for treating OM. Current management strategies for OM, including analgesics, antimicrobial rinses, and growth factor therapies [ , ], primarily offer symptomatic relief but inadequately address the underlying microbial dysbiosis and epithelial metabolic dysfunction. Furthermore, prolonged use of antimicrobial agents can exacerbate microbial resistance and further destabilize the microbiota [ ]. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify treatments that regulate the homeostasis of the oral flora, which is a highly important action for effective therapeutic strategies for OM with few side effects. Chlorogenic acid (CGA), a widely recognized natural polyphenolic compound [ ], has a range of significant pharmacological effects, such as antibacterial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immuno-regulatory effects. CGA can help control the excessive proliferation of opportunistic pathogenic bacteria and maintain the homeostatic balance of the microbiota. The phenolic hydroxyl groups of CGA can noncompetitively inhibit arylamine acetyltransferase activity in bacteria [ ]. This mechanism affects the activity of associated metabolic enzymes, disrupts substance and energy metabolism, and impedes protein synthesis in bacterial strains, thereby suppressing bacterial activity. Moreover, its notable antioxidant activity can prevent chemotherapy-induced oxidative DNA damage in tissue cells [ ]. CGA alleviates mucosal inflammation and epithelial cell damage by inhibiting the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)-cyclic GMP–AMP synthase (CGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signalling pathway [ ]. Although CGA can inhibit the formation of bacterial biofilms in the oral cavity to some extent, its active components are susceptible to decomposition by saliva. Therefore, to meet the needs of OM therapy, we synthesized an integrated biofunctional factor (ZS-NDs) consisting of a spindle-shaped zinc silicate core produced by hydrothermal synthesis, with polyphenol CGA nanoparticles adsorbed on its outer surface through supramolecular assembly. Since the prepared ZS-NDs are stable in both freeze-dried powder and aqueous solution forms, directly applying or spraying them onto the OM lesion site poses challenges in ensuring delivery efficiency and duration of action. Building on our previous strategy for drug delivery using hydrogel dressings [ – ], we prepared a gel via free radical-initiated double-bond polymerization that consisted of gallic acid-modified methacrylated chitosan (CSMA-GA) and methacrylate–PVA (PVAMA). And the introduction of gallic acid (GA) into this hydrogel increased the wet tissue adhesion stability and improved the antioxidant properties of the ZS-NDs [ , ]. Unlike traditional measures, including oral cryotherapy, pharmacological agents (e.g. palifermin, growth factor preparations) and photobiomodulation, hydrogel preparations are not only more convenience and quick-forming but also provide mechanical protection for the ulcer surface (Table ). Furthermore, the hydrogel could be an excellent carrier for ZS-NDs and prolong the drug release period, which is beneficial for wound healing in OM treatment. Here, taking oral microbiota dysbiosis and the metabolic processes in oral mucosal epithelial cells in OM as the entry point, we propose a novel therapeutic nanoplatform (CP@ZS-NDs) targeting the management of the three-level microbiota–microenvironment–host metabolism regulatory network in OM (Scheme ). Through integrated metagenomic–metabolomic analysis, we verified that the oral microbiota dysbiosis caused by OM can lead to changes in metabolic activity in mucosal tissues. CP@ZS-NDs are capable of regulating the homeostasis of the microbiota and maintaining this balance to improve the microenvironment of host epithelial cells. Moreover, CP@ZS-NDs influence carbohydrate metabolism in host oral epithelial cells through regulation of the oral microenvironment by improving the oral microbiome composition. This clarifies that this system aims to modulate the metabolic functions of epithelial cells, thereby promoting the healing of OM. We also preliminary proved that CP@ZS-NDs promote the healing of OM by inhibiting the UDP-galactose-related metabolic pathway and regulating the Integrin α3β1–Fak–Rac1 axis. By bridging microbial ecology and host cell biology, this approach offers a novel, holistic framework for OM treatment, thus allowing us to comprehensively analyse its role in OM and providing a foundation for precise intervention. Results and discussion Oral microbiota dysbiosis caused by OM can lead to changes in metabolic activity in mucosal tissues OM and oral microbiota dysbiosis are intimately related [ ]. To elucidate the interactions between the instances of microbial imbalance in OM and host cells, as well as to explore the specific mechanisms underlying these interactions, we successfully established an animal model of OM in golden hamsters in our early experiments, on the basis of the literature [ – ]. First, we sequenced and analysed oral microbial samples from the animals, and the results indicated a decrease in local microbial diversity accompanied by a significant microbial imbalance (Fig. a). Different alpha diversity indices, including the Simpson index, observed species richness, Shannon index, and Chao index, indicated that ulcerated mucosal tissue harboured a microbiota with a diversity distinct from that of healthy mucosa (Fig. b, S1a-d). PCoA using the Bray–Curtis distance metric was performed to evaluate beta diversity. Comparisons between groups in the dissimilarity analyses revealed that the difference in the microbiome between the healthy mucosa (Control) group and the OM (positive control, P Control) group was extremely significant (Fig. c, S1e-f). The Bray–Curtis distance heatmap revealed that the difference coefficient between the Control and P Control groups was relatively large, suggesting a significant difference in species diversity between the two sample groups (Fig. S1g). Taxonomic and phylogenetic tree analyses revealed that the abundances of microbes in the P Control group were significantly altered compared with those in the Control group (Fig. d). The Wilcoxon rank–sum test was also used to analyse the species differences between the two groups of samples. The abundances of bacteria such as Bacteroides , Rodentibacter , Stomatobaculum , Streptococcus , and Veillonella were significantly greater in the P Control group than in the Control group (Fig. S2, 3). These findings confirm that OM can induce changes in the oral mucosa microenvironment, thereby triggering microbiota dysbiosis, consistent with previous findings [ ]. OM pathogenesis is intricately tied to the dysregulation of oral microbiota homeostasis and epithelial barrier function [ ]. To further elucidate the relationships between microbial disruption and the oral mucosal epithelium, we further conducted nontargeted metabolomics analysis on mucosal tissues affected by OM (Fig. a). The metabolite volcano plot indicated that compared with that in normal oral mucosal tissues, the composition of metabolites in mucosal tissues affected by OM differed significantly (Fig. e). The Mantel test and Procrustes analysis revealed a correlation between the compositional structure of the sample microbial community and the compositional structure of the metabolites (Fig. f). It has been proven that galectin-3 has common properties associated with matricellular proteins because it recognizes β-galactosides [ , ], which are correlated with the UDP-galactose-related metabolic pathway. chunks.content: 1 Introduction Our world is becoming increasingly aged, approximately 1.4 billion people aged 60 and above in 2022, and it is expected that this number will double globally by 2050 ( ). The growing aging population has exacerbated health challenges related to aging, the overall muscle capacity decreases in elderly individuals, including the pelvic floor, partially leads to the occurrence of urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, and constipation ( ; ; ; ; ). There are various reasons for elderly people to develop urinary and defecation dysfunction, one of which is that the excretion of feces and urine is controlled and regulated by the neuromuscular system. For elderly individuals who have not completely lost urinary and fecal control, five physical rehabilitation methods, including exercise training, magnetic stimulation, electrical stimulation, vibration stimulation, and biofeedback, have been shown to enhance pelvic floor muscle strength and improve urinary and defecation dysfunction ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ). For muscle rehabilitation training for elderly people with different types of urinary and defecation dysfunction, a “one size fits all” strategy should not be used. Personalization is a extremely important issue ( ; ; ; ). Taking constipation as an example, strategies based on individual risk factors of elderly constipation patients have been proven to reduce the occurrence of constipation ( ). However, the muscle prioritization for the rehabilitation of elderly individuals with urinary and defecation dysfunction is still not fully understood. It is necessary to explore the quantitative relationship between different rehabilitation training methods and urinary and defecation control ability, in order to provide guidance for personalized rehabilitation training practices. Finite element analysis (FEA) is an appropriate research methodology for investigating complex relationships between rehabilitation training and pelvic floor function, as it is capable of precisely simulating pelvic floor complex structures and intricate biomechanical behaviors. One of the key advantages of the FEA is that it eliminates the need for human experimentation, thereby ensuring a high level of safety, while also facilitating the execution of numerous experiments. For instance, muscle parameters were varied to observe the corresponding changes in outcome indicators. This approach is not only cost-effective but also highly efficient ( ; ). As an advanced tool for biomechanical research, FEA has been widely applied in obstetrics and gynecology, highlighting its contributions in simulating pelvic floor dysfunctions ( ). Notable studies have simulated female pelvic floor analysis ( ; ), pelvic organ prolapses in women ( ; ; ), urethral support functions ( ), levator ani muscle injuries during vaginal delivery and pelvic floor disorders ( ), and the mechanical mechanisms of posterior vaginal prolapse ( ). These previous applications have contributed to the development of pelvic floor simulation models for elderly individuals. Other studies ( ; ; ; ) have developed pelvic floor models for female individuals aged 55, 63, and 70 years. However, these existing finite element models are limited to simulating the pelvic floor muscles and tissues neglecting the abdominal, hip, and back muscles, which are critical for rehabilitation training beyond the pelvic floor and play significant roles in urinary and fecal control. Consequently, the current female pelvic floor finite element models offer limited representation of the full spectrum of muscles involved in urination and defecation. Furthermore, these models typically do not address the unique anatomical and physiological characteristics of elderly populations. Few studies have focused on rehabilitation outcomes and the role of muscle prioritization, especially in elderly women with pelvic floor dysfunctions. Therefore, a more comprehensive composite model is needed, one that integrates not only pelvic floor muscles but also abdominal, hip, and back muscles, to provide more accurate rehabilitation guidance tailored for elderly women. We previously established to establish a finite element model in elderly males, using FEA to explore the quantitative relationship between different rehabilitation training methods and urinary and defecatory control ability ( ). The research findings can elucidate the muscle prioritization for rehabilitation training in elderly men suffering from various types of urinary and defecation dysfunction. However, marked physiological and anatomical differences exist between male and female pelvic floors. For example, women have a greater colonic length, a larger rectal cross-sectional area, and lack a prostate but possess female-specific structures such as the uterus, vagina, urethral detrusor muscle and urethrovaginal sphincter. This study aims to clarify the relationship between muscle function in elderly women and rehabilitation training, prioritizing the identification of key muscles essential for urinary and defecatory rehabilitation. As early as 2011, constructed a FEA of the pelvis and levator ani muscles by performing pelvic CT and MRI scans on healthy elderly nulliparous female volunteers. This approach avoided the disadvantage of relying on cadaveric specimen dissection previously used to obtain models. This study aims to collect CT and MRI data from a normal elderly female volunteer and establish a composite finite element model of the pelvic floor. Following the model construction, the study will conduct quantitative validation of the finite element model, to ensure its validity and guarantee the accuracy of the finite element analysis. Similar to the validation method used in the Peng Y’S study ( ), we compared whether the Valsalva movement process simulated by the patient’s finite element model and the Valsalva movement in the patient’s actual dynamic MRI produced consistent changes (including ARA, RVA, and waist circumference) as a validation method. Muscle material properties, such as the material modulus, are typically related to their physical characteristics. The material modulus describes the ability of muscles to deform under force. Research indicates that the material properties of muscles, including the elastic modulus, may change following rehabilitation training ( ; ). Muscle contraction can cause changes in the internal structure of muscles, increasing their resistance to deformation, reflected in an increase in elastic modulus ( ; ; ; ). Under various simulation plans of FEA, the study will proportionally alter muscle material properties to simulate the rehabilitation effects of five physical therapy methods ( ; ; ). For the observed outcome measures, this study selected retrovesical angle (RVA) and anorectal angulation (ARA), which are used to assess the ability of elderly individuals to voluntarily control urination and defecation ( ; ). Studies have shown differences in the mechanical properties of pelvic soft tissues between elderly and younger populations, with potential variations in material properties ( ). Based on these findings, we made gradual adjustments to the material properties of the pelvic floor muscles to reflect the expected biomechanical changes with aging. These adjustments were made incrementally until the differences between the finite element model and dynamic MRI measurements of ARA, RVA, and waist circumference were within 10%. This process ensured that the model accurately simulated the physiological changes that occur with aging. Due to the complexity and irregularity of structures in the human body, an unstructured meshing approach was adopted for volumetric mesh generation, resulting in a model with a mixed mesh of tetrahedral and hexahedral elements. This hybrid meshing approach leverages the advantages of both element types. Tetrahedral meshes offer greater flexibility in handling complex geometries, while hexahedral meshes generally provide higher computational efficiency and accuracy during numerical simulations. Compared with previous studies that focused solely on pelvic floor muscles, this research firstly developed a comprehensive 3D pelvic-thigh model in elderly women. The findings highlight the critical role of integrating muscle groups beyond the pelvic floor, including the abdominal, hip, and back muscles, in maintaining control of urination and defecation and achieving functional recovery. This comprehensive approach enhances the practical relevance of the study. In constructing the present model, a healthy elderly female dataset was deliberately selected to provide a geometrically intact baseline for biomechanical simulation. In this study, the elastic modulus of muscles was proportionally adjusted to approximate rehabilitation-induced adaptations within a finite element framework. Studies have shown that the elastic modulus is associated with neuromuscular control ( ; ), and rehabilitation training not only alters the active contractile capacity of muscles but also induces passive mechanical changes, which can be observed at both the single-fiber and fiber-bundle levels ( ; ). In addition, oportional modulation of material parameters has also been adopted in previous FEA studies ( ), supporting its feasibility as an exploratory strategy. The model extends beyond traditional pelvic floor simulations because it was constructed based on data from dynamic MRI, CT, and static MRI data, and its accuracy was validated through geometric comparison with key anatomical landmarks, including the waistline, RVA, and ARA. While the model showed good geometric agreement with key pelvic floor anatomical structures, the observed waistline variation of 8.28% was slightly higher than anticipated. This discrepancy can be attributed to the complex nature of soft tissue deformation, which may explain the larger variation observed in waist circumference compared to ARA and RVA. The resulting model showed good geometric agreement with key pelvic floor anatomical structures in a representative elderly female, supporting its preliminary applicability in simulating pelvic biomechanics. These findings suggest potential utility for understanding mechanisms underlying urinary and fecal control, although broader validation is needed. The study employed RVA and ARA as the sole indicators for assessing urinary and fecal control. While RVA and ARA are significant imaging biomarkers, urinary and defecation dysfunction are complex clinical symptoms whose severity is closely linked to patient subjective experience, quality of life, and neural control. Alterations in these two parameters alone do not fully capture the comprehensive clinical functional enhancement. In this study, RVA and ARA served as the primary outcome measures because they are the most readily quantifiable biomechanical indicators within the finite element modeling framework. Thus RVA and ARA should be interpreted as surrogate biomechanical markers rather than comprehensive clinical endpoints. For the first time, this study provides preliminary evidence on the potential muscle prioritization of pelvic floor rehabilitation benefits for elderly women. For constipation management, computational findings suggest that rehabilitation targeting the levator ani muscle might be prioritized when muscle properties fall below baseline levels (1 time), while cases with above-baseline muscle properties may benefit more from comprehensive pelvic floor muscle engagement. Regarding fecal incontinence, sub-baseline muscle conditions suggest the need for integrated training targeting pelvic floor muscles along with rectus abdominis, and erector spinae muscles, whereas supra-baseline conditions may warrant concentrated pelvic floor muscle rehabilitation. For urinary incontinence cases, combined pelvic-hip muscles rehabilitation appears advantageous regardless of baseline muscle status. These observed associations between muscle material coefficients and rehabilitation outcomes highlight the importance of condition-specific muscle prioritization in elderly women’s pelvic rehabilitation, these findings may contribute to the development of more tailored rehabilitation nursing recommendations. It should be emphasized that our interpretation focused on the general trends observed when material properties were below or above baseline, rather than the extreme values of parameter variation. The broader range (0.05–2.0) was applied primarily to test model robustness, while clinical rehabilitation is unlikely to reach such extremes. Recent clinical research by demonstrated that hip exercises alone, as well as combined abdominal, hip, and pelvic floor muscles training, significantly enhance pelvic floor muscle activity. These findings are consistent with our simulation-based results, which suggest that pelvic floor-hip combined training may offer more comprehensive benefits for elderly women with urinary incontinence. In contrast, clinical and imaging studies directly addressing the prioritization of specific muscle groups in constipation and fecal incontinence rehabilitation are limited. Currently, research on pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) for elderly women primarily focuses on the overall efficacy of PFMT, rather than the sequence or prioritization of individual muscle group interventions. Anatomically, the pelvic floor muscles in women are more vulnerable, as they are heavily influenced by pregnancy and childbirth. Striking an appropriate balance between model fidelity and practical feasibility remains a critical and ongoing challenge ( ). It is important to acknowledge certain limitations of this study. First, in this study, muscle elastic modulus was linearly scaled to represent rehabilitation-induced functional improvement. This approach, while a common simplification in finite element modeling, primarily reflects changes in passive stiffness rather than improvements in active contraction capacity or neuromuscular coordination. As such, our method more closely simulates muscle dynamic alterations such as fibrosis than genuine training-induced strengthening. In reality, rehabilitation induces complex bioadaptive processes that include neuromuscular control, motor unit recruitment, muscle fiber type conversion, and myofascial coordination, which cannot be fully represented by a single parameter such as passive stiffness. Therefore, our finite element results should be interpreted as reflecting the structural potential of muscle strengthening, rather than capturing the entire spectrum of functional adaptations. Future studies combining finite element modeling with electrophysiological measurements and clinical outcomes are needed to provide a more comprehensive understanding. By employing FEA, this study delved into the mechanisms underlying the enhancement of urinary and defecation control in the elderly women and identified the differing muscle prioritization for rehabilitation training in elderly men and women. These findings facilitate the personalized recommendation of pelvic floor rehabilitation plans tailored to the muscle condition and dysfunction type of elderly women. The current simplified model was developed from a single elderly female subject, which limits its generalizability. Therefore, it is imperative that future work should focus on developing multi-subject and multi-sample models that account for anatomical and physiological variability. Additionally, clinical validation trials should be undertaken to ensure the broader applicability of rehabilitation strategies.
